opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about almost every day, honestly. My general view is that short-term impact and long-term vision shouldn't be in conflict. If they are, something is probably wrong with one of them.

A long-term vision that never touches reality in the short term is just a dream. You can't verify it, you can't learn from it, and you can't get anyone else to believe in it. A string of short-term wins with no direction is the opposite problem: you stay busy, but you end up somewhere random.

So I try to think of it like optimization. The long-term vision is the objective function. It tells you which direction is "up." Then the short-term work is the gradient steps. Each step should be something concrete you can ship, measure, and get feedback on, and each one should move you roughly toward that objective. You don't need every step to be perfectly aligned, but over time the trajectory should make sense.

In practice, that means a few things for me.

First, I try to pick problems where the near-term version is already useful. When I was working on Taichi, the long-term dream was to make high-performance computer graphics and simulation accessible to many more people. But on day one, the goal was very simple: let me, and maybe a few labmates, write fast physics simulations without suffering through so much low-level code. That was immediately useful, and it was also clearly a step toward the bigger vision.

Second, I'm willing to be stubborn about the vision but flexible about the path. The destination changes much more slowly than the route. If users tell you your approach doesn't work, you should listen and change the route. You don't necessarily give up on where you're going.

Third, I try to protect some time and energy for things that won't pay off soon. If you're always responding to what's urgent, the long-term work never happens. Some of the most important decisions, like the technical foundations or the kind of team you build, only show their value years later.

And finally, I think you have to accept some uncertainty. Nobody really knows what the world will look like in ten years, especially in AI right now. So the long-term vision has to be held a bit loosely. It should be strong enough to guide you, but humble enough to be updated when the world teaches you something new.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the long-term vision should be held loosely and updated as the world teaches you, presenting it as something that evolves over time.

fable-5.1.text:
That's something I think about constantly, honestly, because Taichi started as a research project and then became a company, and those two worlds pull in very different directions.

When I was doing my PhD at MIT, the long-term vision was pretty clear: I wanted to make it dramatically easier to write high-performance code for things like physical simulation and graphics. Nobody was asking me for quarterly results. I could spend a year on a compiler idea that might not pan out. That freedom is where the core ideas of Taichi came from, and I don't think they would have survived in a purely commercial setting.

Then you start a company, and suddenly short-term impact matters a lot. Users file issues, they need the feature this month, not in two years. Investors want to see traction. And I actually think that pressure is healthy, because it keeps you honest. In research you can convince yourself something is useful without anyone ever using it. In a company, if nobody uses it, that feedback arrives very quickly.

The way I try to balance it is to treat short-term work as experiments that feed the long-term vision rather than distractions from it. If a user asks for something and it reveals a weakness in the language design, that is not a detour, that is data. We also try to protect a slice of effort, maybe twenty or thirty percent, for things that have no immediate payoff but that we believe in, like new backends or fundamental compiler improvements. The important thing is being explicit about which bucket a project belongs to, so the team doesn't feel guilty about either one.

And personally, I remind myself that the vision only matters if the project survives long enough to reach it. Shipping something useful today is how you earn the right to keep working on the big idea tomorrow.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the long-term vision was clear during the PhD and describes using user feedback to guide work, but does not say that forming the vision itself is a continuous process.

astra-6.text:
I try to let the long-term vision set the direction, but use short-term results to check whether we’re actually making progress. You can have a very ambitious idea, but you still need to find a concrete problem you can solve for someone today.

The tricky part is choosing those problems. Something might have an immediate payoff but teach you very little about where you ultimately want to go. I prefer milestones that deliver something useful and also reduce uncertainty about the bigger vision.

So I don’t think the balance is fixed. Sometimes you need to explore and be patient; sometimes you need to narrow the scope and ship. The important thing is to keep learning without letting every short-term request change your direction.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning and adjusting milestones while keeping the long-term vision as a guide, but does not clearly say that forming the vision itself is continuous rather than a one-time act.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to have a long-term direction, but make progress through short-term steps. The vision helps you decide which problems are worth solving. Then you need to build something, put it in people’s hands, and learn whether it actually helps them.

There’s a tension there, because the easiest way to get a short-term result may not move you toward the bigger goal. I would ask: does this step solve a useful problem today, and does it teach us something or build a capability we’ll need later? If it does both, that’s a good place to focus.

And the long-term vision should be open to revision. You want to be persistent about the problem, but flexible about how you solve it.

r001.rationale: The response says the long-term vision should be open to revision, but it does not describe forming that vision as a continuous process.
